findings: Distinguishes forecasts, single structural shocks and replacement of a policy rule; Gaussian rotations and temporal aggregation expose nonidentification rather than mere predictive error.

Derives the direct-IV ratio, Gaussian quadratic-form CLT and explicit-bandwidth covariance argument. Weak normalization retains unbounded/disconnected sets; the VAR challenger carries fitted-dynamics uncertainty.

Separated-block learning has explicit coupling, nuisance-product and accumulated covariance-error bounds. Lasso rates, common calendar shocks and stationary-change reconstruction retain their additional restrictions.

Funding value includes the repricing cost on induced first-month balances and cross-horizon covariance. The comparison keeps fixed policy and nuisance-training information, failed coverage, weak/inadmissible instruments and misspecification visible.
Dynamic solvability and separation claims are tied to their source conditions; the conjectural cyclic d-separation calculus is not promoted to an established result.
Exact sampling and the oscillatory alias distinguish drift identification from numerical integration. Rule-intercept and clamped-rate interventions have different equilibrium responses.
Event weighting retains waiting-time integrals, mean-one regularity and the intervention filtration. Changing visit marks, visit intensity and deterministic regimes remain different targets.
The restricted martingale-gradient derivation states its tangent-space limits; the no-event filter carries the information in silence and removes a replaced observation mechanism under intervention.

conclusion: No consequential new defect established in these complete rendered-text contexts. The original time-series/dependence/observation objections have developed bounded arguments. Independent correctness, proportionality and visual acceptance remain open.
